numerical_failure.observed_behavior: With skipna=False, nanmedian's short-circuit returns a bare np.nan; the 2-D path (np.apply_along_axis) takes output dtype from the first slice so one column holding a missing value casts every later column to float64, discarding the imaginary part of complex columns. Example: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1 + 2j, np.nan], "b": [1 + 2j, 3 + 4j]}); df.median(skipna=False)["b"] gives 2.0. In _get_counts_nanvar, once ddof >= count, count and d are replaced by bare Python floats, so nansem widens a float32 result to float64 in the 1-D path.
numerical_failure.expected_behavior: df.median(skipna=False)["b"] should be 2+3j, same as df[["b", "a"]].median(skipna=False)["b"]; missing values should be returned in the input's own dtype (dtype's own NaN), so float32 stays float32 and columns are not widened.
trigger_conditions: nanmedian called with skipna=False and a missing value present in one column (2-D DataFrame path)
column order matters: the discrepancy depends on where the column holding a missing value sits
complex-valued columns whose median is well-defined
_get_counts_nanvar reached with ddof >= count (nansem/nanvar 1-D path) on float32 input
oracle_clues: Reproducer in PR#68487 compares the two column orderings; the reordered result is the correct reference
Release note states Series.median returned a real NaN for complex data in the same case
Fix makes missing values use the input's own dtype, so float32 results stay float32

numerical_characteristics.dtype: complex128 input (complex columns); float32 input for nansem/nanvar path; float16 mentioned for mean/sum overflow in a separate whatsnew entry
numerical_characteristics.precision: float32 result widened to float64 in the 1-D path while 2-D stayed float32; complex imaginary part discarded when cast to float64
category_specific_evidence: Reproducer: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1 + 2j, np.nan], "b": [1 + 2j, 3 + 4j]}); df.median(skipna=False)["b"] returns 2.0 (imaginary part lost), while df[["b","a"]].median(skipna=False)["b"] returns 2+3j for the same data in the other column order.

Violated property: the median of column b ([1+2j, 3+4j]) should be 2+3j (complex median preserved); result depends on column order because np.apply_along_axis takes output dtype from the first slice, which is the column containing NaN.
Commit: nanmedian skipna=False short-circuit returned bare np.nan; the 2-D path via np.apply_along_axis cast later columns to float64.
Commit: _get_counts_nanvar replaced count and d with Python floats when ddof >= count, widening float32 nansem result to float64 in 1-D path; fixed so missing values carry input dtype.
Test test_nanops: values np.array([1,2,3], dtype=dtype) with ddof; asserts result.dtype == values.dtype for both 1-D and 2-D (axis=1) inputs.

Test test_median_skipna_false_keeps_complex parametrized over na_first in [True, False], asserting df.median(skipna=False) and df.T.median(axis=1, skipna=False) yield expected Series with complex(np.nan) or 2+3j.
Series.median returned a real NaN for complex data in the same case (per whatsnew entry).
GH#68194 test: describe computing std raised for every SparseDtype Series; fix aligns SparseDtype columns with dense results.
reproduction_risks: Column order sensitivity: the bug only appears when the NaN-holding column is reduced first; reproduction must test both orders.
Expected NaN for complex must be complex(np.nan), not real NaN, when comparing.
Sparse dtype comparison may need check_dtype=False for describe-based tests, per the test_diff note.
